how: Invitations recruit flag workers and ask members to build, finish and defend shared work.
Questions receive explanations of placement controls and the timer, while latecomers ask what the event meant.
Participants judge dispersed projects ineffective and doubt that one defender can hold the threatened work alone.
A short reply reports doing a part of the avocado without asking for anything back.
An avocado proposal receives a reply reporting personal placement and near completion.
A late-shift defender receives a short commitment to help, while a separate help request receives a reasoned refusal.
A participant forgives a misplaced pixel after anger, showing interpersonal repair rather than a demonstrated collective withdrawal.
Members propose flags, coordinates, slogans and later additions while disputing their suitability.
Proposing or mapping the flag instantiates the starter independently of whether others subsequently join.
An organizing proposal gathers participants who supply a practicable flag plan without establishing a permanent leader.
Participants report starting, repainting, aligning and completing portions of shared work.
Coordinates, spreadsheets and templates returned from Discord guide collective placement.
Participants route planning into Discord, return templates and a reported vote, and require projects to become official there.
A published template does not settle execution unless keepers recognize the current intended design.
One proposed addition is routed into a bot template, making automation part of design implementation.
A reported vote and official-project demands connect backstage routing to locally decided order.
A proposed division of labour, a reported vote and collective-approval demands instantiate decided episodes without testing the cross-room frequency claim.
Maintained bots, scripts and alternate accounts augment placements and receive retrospective credit for defense.
Automation uptake depends on source trust and whether participants value stable output over manual change.
Maintenance scripts are visible, but no coded turn establishes an interval-limited shortage causing their adoption.
A script is explicitly offered to keep the flag alive without establishing why automation was first adopted.
Device knowledge, late shifts and returning workers or sleepers condition when participants can help or implement a decision.
Participants report stale canvas state and refreshing, which can make apparent sabotage an interface-related misunderstanding.
Participants clear stray pixels, align geometry and share defensive shifts, but keepers also erase unfamiliar planned additions as damage.
The avocado completion announcement immediately turns to keeping vandals away.
Participants inspect pixel ownership, accuse named users, deny responsibility and identify mistaken attribution.
Repairers challenge accusations by diagnosing stale display state and revising the apparent meaning of pixel ownership.
A reported stale display supplies an explicit alternative explanation for apparent vandalism and prompts revision of blame.
Participants compare coordinates, reject exposed locations and recommend leaving a spot before the approaching neighbour overruns it.
One participant redirects effort from a flag being destroyed to an existing flag near Argentina.
Capacity doubts and moves are visible separately, but no coded turn attributes relocation to too few hands.
Participants negotiate cessions, merged borders and nonexpansion agreements with neighbours.
A reported war and ongoing raids are answered by a negotiated cession for future support and peace.
Help exchanges include conditional bargains, reciprocal repair, thanks and refusals based on competing commitments.
The open-border proposal elicits a help condition and a narrower promise to erase the hostile score.
The urgent repair request receives an immediate promise, but the helper had already offered assistance, leaving shortage-initiated contact unestablished.
A participant recounts a three-country coalition rebuilding and maintaining the flags together.
The coalition narrator explicitly credits the hostile score attack with uniting the three-country defense.
Participants refuse raids by invoking existing peace, ongoing neighbour repairs or the value of leaving others' art intact.
A refusal invokes an earlier peace agreement as the reason not to attack the neighbour.
Attack calls receive refusals explaining that the room must finish its work or spare neighbours who are repairing it.
A declaration of war is answered with an already existing peace agreement.
Calling erasure of others' art objectionable supports leaving it intact and proposing an alternative design.
The evidence supports contested concessions and refusal of ally restraint, not an explicit rule that representatives cannot bind every placer.
An existing-alliance reminder is answered with insistence on destroying the ally, fitting after-agreement refusal rather than an explicit disclaimer of representative standing.
Visitors explicitly present themselves as diplomats or delegates carrying proposals for their communities.
Guests ask to use host territory while participants require collective approval or consultation with owners of neighbouring work.
Competing project preferences do not establish that a speaker belongs to both rooms in a contest.
Football rivalry supplies the target and rationale in the same turn proposing damage to national signs.
Football and national rivalries enter the canvas through score jokes and calls to overwrite rival flags.
Colonial memory, national stereotypes and inherited jokes give designs and help requests meanings beyond their pixels.
Participants make new jokes from the bloc, the armed-looking Jesus and changes to BUNDA, and reuse the Void as a political comparison.
A canvas-born comparison is carried into ordinary political news rather than staying inside canvas discussion.
Participants refuse a swastika proposal as bad taste and ask moderators to remove hateful comments without establishing universal compliance.
An Argentina-themed takeover licenses copied styling and mock Spanish alongside the separate canvas game.
Flood complaints prompt routing toward a canvas sub while participants dispute the value of repetitive flag discussion.
A dedicated Brazilian canvas discussion sub is announced and later adopted as a destination without demonstrating an autonomous faction's internal organization.
A complaint explicitly names flooding as the reason for a dedicated sub and receives the existing destination.
The observed turn threatens self-sabotage in response to complaints without establishing execution or that posting fatigue caused the threat.
Completion and victory stories solicit pride, thanks, personal contribution claims and competing allocations of credit.
The maker marks the completed avocado with an explicit collective achievement announcement.
A visitor thanks the room for shared character art and receives a repair invitation without establishing subscriptions or durable membership.
A speculative poster or museum future does not establish approaching creators, companies or the press for notice.
Participants save the canvas, share final images and timelapses, and reconstruct a record of its changes.
Preservation during placement and at closure is visible, but no coded exchange establishes celebration as its causal trigger.
Participants correct omitted episodes and simplified battle accounts and share cleaned work within the revised range of single-account corrections.
Compilers diagnose unavailable earlier data and recover snapshots, scripts and incremental differences to rebuild missing history.
Participants propose a larger successor flag, another canvas and continuing alliances or cultural exchanges without documenting their completion.
Continuation proposals appear alongside records, but the record does not establish that preserving the work caused them.
A participant explicitly marks a return to ordinary programming rather than preserving or extending the canvas organization.
Participants raid, annex territory and convert neighbouring signs into rival slogans or their own words.
The challenge posed by Argentina's flag receives a reply reporting direct placement over it.
Retrospectives claim victory over named enemies and blame repeated score attacks without independently verifying attribution.
Named-enemy retrospectives occur, but the coded exchanges do not establish the proposed attack-to-contest-talk mechanism as a distinct causal transition.
A participant retrospectively claims infiltration of the opponent's voice chat and a resulting ban without independently establishing its effect on victory.
